title: Bangladesh Measles Death Toll Crosses 900 as Vaccination Gaps Persist
excerpt: The outbreak, one of Bangladesh's worst public health crises in years, has infected more than 141,000 people since March, with children under five bearing the brunt of a preventable disease.
body:
• Bangladesh's measles death toll has surpassed 900, with over 17,800 confirmed and 141,776 suspected cases since mid-March 2026
  • More than 82% of those infected are children under five, with over half of all deaths occurring in infants under nine months who are too young for routine vaccination
  • Experts blame political instability, halted vaccine funding under the previous interim government, and COVID-era disruptions for critical immunity gaps
  • An emergency vaccination campaign targeting 18 million children has been underway since April, but public health officials say herd immunity remains out of reach

A Preventable Crisis Deepens

Bangladesh's devastating measles outbreak has now claimed more than 900 lives, making it one of the country's worst public health emergencies in recent memory. According to the latest data from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), the combined toll of confirmed and suspected measles deaths stood at 902 as of mid-August, with 17,800 laboratory-confirmed infections and more than 141,776 suspected cases recorded since the outbreak began in mid-March.

The crisis has overwhelmed hospitals across the country. More than 121,000 patients have been hospitalized since March 15, though roughly 116,800 have since recovered and been discharged. The overall fatality rate stands at 2.93%, but the rate among confirmed cases is a stark 5.21%, underscoring the severity of infections that progress beyond initial symptoms.

Children Bear the Heaviest Burden

The outbreak has been particularly devastating for the youngest and most vulnerable. Health Minister Sardar Shakhawat Hossain Bokul told parliament that 82% of those infected are children under five years old. Research from the DGHS shows that 80% of children admitted to hospitals were unvaccinated, and more than half of all deaths have occurred in infants under nine months — children too young to receive routine measles vaccination.

"This resurgence highlights critical immunity gaps, particularly among zero-dose and under-vaccinated children, while infections among infants under nine months, who are not yet eligible for routine vaccination, are especially alarming."

— Rana Flowers, UNICEF Representative in Bangladesh

The Dhaka division has recorded the highest toll, with more than 57,400 suspected cases and 9,825 confirmed infections, followed by Chittagong with over 23,700 suspected cases. The Sylhet division, despite a smaller population, has reported 110 suspected deaths — among the highest per capita rates in the country.

How Vaccination Coverage Collapsed

Bangladesh had made significant progress in measles control over decades. Between 2014 and 2015, nationwide measles-rubella campaigns vaccinated more than 50 million children, and by the mid-2010s, first-dose coverage exceeded 92%. The country's vaccination rate rose from 2% in 1979 to 81.6% — a remarkable achievement, but still short of the 95% threshold the World Health Organization says is necessary to achieve herd immunity.

Public health experts point to a cascade of failures. The COVID-19 pandemic diverted resources and attention away from routine immunization. Then, political instability during the interim government of Muhammad Yunus compounded the problem, with vaccine procurement disrupted and funding halted. A report by the Canada-based Global Centre for Democratic Governance described the outbreak as predictable from an epidemiological standpoint, noting that the crisis was "not an unexpected event."

Prof. Mahmudur Rahman, former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research, estimates that more than four million children remain unvaccinated — a gap large enough to sustain transmission indefinitely.

Emergency Response and Global Context

The government launched an emergency measles-rubella vaccination campaign on April 5, targeting children aged six months to five years across 18 high-risk districts. The campaign, supported by WHO, UNICEF, and the Gavi vaccine alliance, aims to immunize 18 million children and has since expanded nationwide in phases.

The Bangladesh crisis comes amid a broader global resurgence of measles. The United States has recorded more than 2,000 cases in 2026, the highest in years, driven by declining vaccination rates in some communities. The WHO has warned that measles outbreaks are increasing worldwide as pandemic-era disruptions continue to erode immunization coverage.

For the Indian diaspora, the Bangladesh outbreak carries particular resonance. The two countries share a long border and extensive people-to-people ties, and public health officials across South Asia have raised concerns about cross-border transmission risks.

What Comes Next

Despite months of emergency vaccination efforts, the outbreak shows no signs of abating. Daily case counts remain above 900, and an average of three to five children continue to die each day. Health officials say the campaign must reach every unvaccinated child, including those in remote areas missed by earlier drives.

The challenge now is not just medical but logistical and political. Experts say sustained funding, community-level micro-planning, and early isolation of patients — rather than reliance on hospital-based ICU treatment — are essential to bending the curve. For a country that once stood as a model for immunization success in South Asia, the outbreak is a painful reminder of how quickly hard-won progress can unravel.
nri_angle: Bangladesh shares extensive ties with India and the broader South Asian diaspora; the outbreak underscores global vaccination gaps that affect communities worldwide.
